key_insight: This paper shows that models can learn to reason more efficiently by learning confidence signals, without explicitly being trained to stop early. A self-supervised confidence objective can produce substantial reductions in reasoning length while preserving performance.
problem_solved: Reasoning models often generate unnecessarily long chains of thought, which increases latency and compute cost at inference time. Prior solutions usually rely on explicit early-stopping rules or training with length penalties, both of which can be brittle or require direct supervision of when to stop.
method: Train a confidence predictor using a self-supervised procedure rather than direct stop labels.
Use confidence as a proxy signal for deciding when further reasoning is unlikely to help.
Improve inference efficiency without explicitly optimizing for shorter traces or adding length-based reinforcement rewards.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical path to cheaper and faster reasoning models without sacrificing accuracy. It suggests that better uncertainty/confidence modeling can be leveraged as an efficiency tool, not just a calibration metric.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing self-supervised confidence training feeding into reasoning models
Before/after comparison of long reasoning traces vs shortened traces
Bar chart of compute or token usage versus task accuracy
Icon set illustrating confidence, stopping, and efficiency gains
paper_title: Learning to Stop without Learning to Stop: Self-Supervised Confidence Training Improves Reasoning Efficiency
paper_authors: Parsa Hosseini, Akasha Tigalappanavara, Sumit Nawathe, Chenrui Fan, Sourya Basu
